explanations.explanation: Maker is the word. The LORD calls Himself the One "…who formed you from the womb…" (Isaiah 44:2). Jacob is the name He uses here for His people. He also says He is the One "…who will help you…", and I'd say that's a pretty good way to start a message.

Judge is a fair guess after the heavy words just before this. But in this verse the LORD calls Himself Jacob's Maker, the One who formed him from the womb. Jacob is the name He uses here for His people. Next time, listen for who He says He is to them before you decide what He's about to say.

Shepherd is a lovely word, and the Bible does use it elsewhere: "The LORD is my shepherd…" (Psalm 23:1). Here, though, the LORD calls Himself Jacob's Maker, the One who formed him from the womb. Jacob is the name He uses here for His people. I think I'd have picked Shepherd too, because I love a good sheep picture, but this verse sticks with Maker.

Those are His first words: "Do not be afraid, O Jacob My servant…" (Isaiah 44:2). Look at what came right before, because the LORD had spoken of destruction (Isaiah 43:28). Then He turns around and speaks to Jacob as His servant, the one He has chosen. I think that's a big breath of relief.

I get why you'd brace for that, with those heavy words coming right before (Isaiah 43:28). But look at what the LORD actually says to Jacob here: "Do not be afraid, O Jacob My servant…" (Isaiah 44:2). Jacob is the name He uses for His people. He's calling them His servant and the one He has chosen, so the message turns toward comfort.

That one sounds like a message from a landlord, friend. The text has no such order here. The LORD says, "Do not be afraid, O Jacob My servant…" (Isaiah 44:2). Jacob is the name He uses for His people, and they get comfort first.

The LORD says, "I will pour out My Spirit on your descendants, and My blessing on your offspring." (Isaiah 44:3). Water goes on the dry ground and the Spirit goes on the people. Dry ground doesn't have to do anything but sit there and get soaked. I'd say that's a pretty easy job.

I can see why anger came to mind after all that talk of destruction (Isaiah 43:28). But this verse is a promise of the opposite kind. The LORD says, "I will pour out My Spirit on your descendants, and My blessing on your offspring." Water for dry ground, Spirit and blessing for the people.

Silver would be nice, I won't lie. But the LORD says nothing about silver here. He says, "I will pour out My Spirit on your descendants, and My blessing on your offspring." (Isaiah 44:3). The thirsty land gets water, and the people get something no bank can hold.

It's the other way around, friend. The LORD says, "They will sprout among the grass like willows by flowing streams." (Isaiah 44:4). That's a picture of growing and thriving, not wilting. Nobody sprouts like a willow by a stream while drying up in the heat.

Right, the text says the opposite of wilting. The LORD says, "They will sprout among the grass like willows by flowing streams." (Isaiah 44:4). That's a picture of growing, with water close by. Water was just promised in the verse before, so the willows are set up well.

The text says still another "…will write on his hand, ‘The LORD’s,’…" (Isaiah 44:5). A hand is right where he can see it all day. Three people, three ways of saying the same thing: they belong to the LORD. I'd have a tough time with this one, since I'm all mustache and no hands.

A door is a fair guess, since people do put names on doors. But the text puts the writing somewhere closer. Still another "…will write on his hand, ‘The LORD’s,’…" (Isaiah 44:5). The mark goes on the person himself, not on his house.

I see why you went high, but the text says lower. Still another "…will write on his hand, ‘The LORD’s,’…" (Isaiah 44:5). Forehead is not mentioned here. The hand is the spot, and he'd see it every time he reached for something.
The text says the opposite, friend. Right after "I am the first and I am the last…" the LORD says, “…and there is no God but Me.” (Isaiah 44:6). Nothing in that sentence puts another god beside Him.

Yes, it's False. The LORD says, “I am the first and I am the last, and there is no God but Me.” (Isaiah 44:6). Right after calling Himself the first and the last, He says there is no God but Him. No other god is named beside Him in that line.

He asks, “Have I not told you and declared it long ago?” (Isaiah 44:8). He's saying His people already heard it from Him. Anyone who wants to match Him has to foretell what's coming, and He says He already did. I'd like to see somebody try to top that, friend.

The text goes the other direction. The LORD asks, “Have I not told you and declared it long ago?” (Isaiah 44:8). Nothing here says He kept it hidden. He told His people and declared it, which is the whole point of the challenge.

A dream makes for a nice story, but this verse doesn't mention one. The LORD asks, “Have I not told you and declared it long ago?” (Isaiah 44:8). The words are told and declared, and the text doesn't say how. So we stay with what it gives us.

He tells them, “You are My witnesses!” (Isaiah 44:8). Right after saying "Do not tremble or fear." He gives them a job. A witness is somebody who can say what they've seen and heard. I think that's a pretty big honor to be handed in the middle of a worry.

Judges sit up high and make the rulings, but that's not the title here. The LORD tells His people, “You are My witnesses!” (Isaiah 44:8). A witness tells what they know. The LORD is the One who asks, "Is there any God but Me?" and the people get to stand and testify.

I see why a fear-not speech might lead to soldiers. But the LORD says something different: “You are My witnesses!” (Isaiah 44:8). A witness is someone who says what's true about what the LORD has told them, friend.
That's right. The LORD says, “There is no other Rock; I know not one.” (Isaiah 44:8). He doesn't just say there's no other. He adds that He knows not one.

It's actually True. The LORD says, “There is no other Rock; I know not one.” (Isaiah 44:8). Those last four words are in the text, so He does add that He knows not one. I'll bet that line is easy to miss when you're reading fast.
The text says their witnesses "…fail to see or comprehend, so they are put to shame." (Isaiah 44:9). Seeing and understanding are what's missing. Those are the two things the verse names.

I can see how that sounds right, since a witness talks. But the text puts the problem in a different place. Their witnesses "…fail to see or comprehend, so they are put to shame." (Isaiah 44:9). The trouble is with seeing and understanding, not with talking.

Stand or walk is a fair guess for something a witness might do. But in this verse, the text is talking about the witnesses. They "…fail to see or comprehend, so they are put to shame." (Isaiah 44:9). It's about what they can see and understand, not about their legs.

The text says, “…for the craftsmen themselves are only human.” (Isaiah 44:11). Human hands made the thing, and humans are the ones putting their trust in it. That's the reason the companions will be put to shame. It's a short reason, and I think it hits hard.

That's a reasonable guess, but the text doesn't say it. The reason it gives is, “…for the craftsmen themselves are only human.” (Isaiah 44:11). Nothing here mentions the Sabbath. The shame comes from who made the thing, not from when they worked.

explanations.answer: They copied the nations around them
explanations.explanation: That sounds believable, but the text doesn't say it. The reason given is, “…for the craftsmen themselves are only human.” (Isaiah 44:11). It doesn't talk about copying anybody. It points at the plain fact that humans made it.

The text says, “Yet he grows hungry and loses his strength; he fails to drink water and grows faint.” (Isaiah 44:12). The man making the god is the one getting tired and worn out. He needs a snack break from his own project, friend. Meanwhile the thing he's building needs nothing.

Proud might fit the mood, but the text names something else. It says, “Yet he grows hungry and loses his strength…” (Isaiah 44:12). It's his body running low, not his attitude. He keeps hammering while his strength drains away.

Wealthy would be a nice reward for all that hammering. But the text says something different. “Yet he grows hungry and loses his strength; he fails to drink water and grows faint.” (Isaiah 44:12). The verse is about his strength, not his money.

The text says he "…fashions it in the likeness of man, like man in all his glory, that it may dwell in a shrine." (Isaiah 44:13). The idol is made to look like a person. So a man makes a thing shaped like a man and then looks to it for help. That's a circle if I ever saw one.

A bull is a fair guess, but this verse says something else. The woodworker "…fashions it in the likeness of man, like man in all his glory, that it may dwell in a shrine." (Isaiah 44:13). This idol is shaped like a person.

An eagle sounds impressive, I'll give you that. But the text says the woodworker "…fashions it in the likeness of man, like man in all his glory, that it may dwell in a shrine." (Isaiah 44:13). No wings here. The shape is a man.

The text says, “He plants a laurel, and the rain makes it grow.” (Isaiah 44:14). The woodworker plants it, but the rain does the growing. Notice he can't take credit for that part. He gets the wood and the rain gets the work.

That makes sense for a careful gardener, but the text gives the credit elsewhere. “He plants a laurel, and the rain makes it grow.” (Isaiah 44:14). The woodworker plants, and the rain makes it grow. He doesn't get to take that part, friend.

Streams do show up in this passage, but with the willows in verse 4. For the laurel, the text says, “He plants a laurel, and the rain makes it grow.” (Isaiah 44:14). The rain is the one doing the work here. No stream is mentioned for this tree.

It's right there in the text. “He takes some of it to warm himself, and he kindles a fire and bakes his bread.” (Isaiah 44:15). The same wood that keeps him warm and bakes his bread is the wood he's about to make into a god. I'd be nervous about that, friend.

It's True. The text says, “He takes some of it to warm himself, and he kindles a fire and bakes his bread.” (Isaiah 44:15). So some of the wood goes to everyday needs, warmth and bread. And then the same wood heads somewhere very different.

The text says, “He also fashions it into a god and worships it; he makes an idol and bows down to it.” (Isaiah 44:15). The same wood that fed his fire becomes the thing he bows to. A tree went from fuel to a thing he worships. I think that should make a person stop and scratch his head.

A door would be a sensible thing to make from wood. The text says something else, though. “He also fashions it into a god and worships it; he makes an idol and bows down to it.” (Isaiah 44:15). No door in this verse, just an idol he bows to.

A bed after all that work sounds nice, friend. But the text doesn't mention one. It says, “He also fashions it into a god and worships it; he makes an idol and bows down to it.” (Isaiah 44:15). The wood becomes something he bows down to instead.

He bows down and prays, “Save me, for you are my god.” (Isaiah 44:17). He's asking to be saved by something made from the leftover wood. The verse before has him warm from the fire on the other half. I think that tells you which half did the useful work.

Warm is close, because he got warm in the verse before. That was from the fire, though, where he said, “Ah! I am warm; I see the fire.” (Isaiah 44:16). In verse 17 he prays to the carved god and says, “Save me, for you are my god.” So he asks to be saved.

Riches would be a natural thing to ask for. But the text records a different prayer. He bows to the carved god and says, “Save me, for you are my god.” (Isaiah 44:17). It's a cry to be saved, not a wish for money.

explanations.answer: Their eyes and minds have been shut
explanations.explanation: The text says, “…He has shut their eyes so they cannot see and closed their minds so they cannot understand.” (Isaiah 44:18). That's the reason this verse gives for why they don't see how foolish it is. It's a hard verse, and I think it's worth sitting with.

explanations.answer: No one ever warned them about it
explanations.explanation: That sounds sensible, but it isn't the reason the text gives. It says, “…He has shut their eyes so they cannot see and closed their minds so they cannot understand.” (Isaiah 44:18). The problem is that they can't see or understand. The verse doesn't say anything about whether anyone warned them.

explanations.answer: Their idols hide the truth from them
explanations.explanation: Idols get blamed for a lot, but the text doesn't say this one. It says, “…He has shut their eyes so they cannot see and closed their minds so they cannot understand.” (Isaiah 44:18). The idols aren't named as the ones hiding anything. The reason given is that their eyes and minds have been shut.

The text says, “He feeds on ashes.” (Isaiah 44:20). Earlier, he burned half of the wood to roast meat and eat (Isaiah 44:16). This verse then says he feeds on ashes, and ashes won't fill anybody, friend.
Dust is a good guess, since it's dry and empty like ashes. But the text says, “He feeds on ashes.” (Isaiah 44:20). Ashes fit because they're what burned wood leaves behind. So it stays with ashes.
Smoke fits the fire scene, I'll give you that. But the text says, “He feeds on ashes.” (Isaiah 44:20). So the word is ashes, not smoke.

It's the other way around. The text says he "…cannot deliver himself…" (Isaiah 44:20). He holds the thing in his right hand and still can't ask whether it's a lie. His deluded heart has led him astray, so he can't see it for himself.

That's right, he can't. The text says he "…cannot deliver himself…" (Isaiah 44:20). The thing is right there in his right hand, and he still can't ask whether it's a lie. His deluded heart has led him astray.

The LORD says, “I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud, and your sins like a mist.” (Isaiah 44:22). Clouds and mist are the kind of thing that clears away. I think that's one of the loveliest lines in the whole passage. It's a gift for Jacob, whom the LORD has called His servant.

It's True, friend. The LORD says, “I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud, and your sins like a mist.” (Isaiah 44:22). The words "…like a cloud…" and "…like a mist." are right in the verse. He's telling Jacob this after calling him His servant.

The LORD says, “Return to Me, for I have redeemed you.” (Isaiah 44:22). The reason is already in the sentence: He has redeemed them. So the door is open before they even take a step. I think anyone would want to come back to that.

Bowing is all over this passage, but this verse asks for something else. The LORD says, “Return to Me, for I have redeemed you.” (Isaiah 44:22). He's calling His people back to Him. The idol makers bowed to wood, and here He says come back.

Praying is a good thing, and the idol maker did pray in verse 17, just to the wrong place. But here the LORD says, “Return to Me, for I have redeemed you.” (Isaiah 44:22). The word is return, and the reason is that He has redeemed them.

The text says, “For the LORD has redeemed Jacob, and revealed His glory in Israel.” (Isaiah 44:23). That's the reason for the song. The heavens are told to sing for joy, the depths of the earth to shout aloud, and the mountains, forests and trees to break forth in song. That's a lot of voices, and I think it's worth listening.

That's a big headline, but it's not in this passage. The reason given for the singing is, “For the LORD has redeemed Jacob, and revealed His glory in Israel.” (Isaiah 44:23). Babylon isn't mentioned in this verse at all. The song is about what the LORD has done.

explanations.answer: The idols have all been burned
explanations.explanation: Burned wood does show up in this passage, but it isn't the reason for the song. The text says, “For the LORD has redeemed Jacob, and revealed His glory in Israel.” (Isaiah 44:23). The singing is about what the LORD did for Jacob. Nothing here says the idols were burned.
